Mr. Speaker, I was under the impression that second reading of any bill dealt with debate on the principle of the bill. I have to ask myself what the principle in Bill C-45 is. How do I square the way I stand and the way my party stands on the principle contained in this bill? I think the principle is one of confrontation.
This has been the pattern since the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) ran for office in 1968. It is reminiscent of a candidate for Prime Minister standing in Montreal waving defiance on St. Jean Baptiste Day, which caused the rest of Canada to say: "What a strong Prime Minister he will make. Look how he puts the rabble in their place. That is the type of man we want as leader". That is the same kind of confrontation which we experienced when the LaPalme drivers were demonstrating on Parliament Hill against the manner in which they had lost their jobs. It is the same kind of principle. The Prime Minister said to working class people who lost their jobs through no fault of their own: "Mange la merde". At the same time, the rest of Canada said: "What a tough Prime Minister! He has moxie, he has backbone. That is the man."

It is the same sort of principle we saw with respect to Quebec and the government of Quebec. It is the same type of confrontation where the Prime Minister is building on a scapegoat philosophy, so that the rest of Canada says: "It takes a French Canadian to put French Canadians in their place". That is the sort of cynicism, that is the kind of philosophy I find when I read this one-page bill. What else is the principle in it?
I was shocked to hear the Postmaster General (Mr. Lamon-tagne) say yesterday in a CBC interview that all this bill does is to provide for CUPW a clause which is already in the Canada Labour Code. Section 181 of the Canada Labour Code says, in effect, that workers who are covered by it cannot go on strike during an election period. Mr. Speaker, he has not read the bill. I phoned up and said: "You have used section 181 but you have not put in section 148," which says, in effect, that the workers who are prevented from striking during an election period will be covered by the previous collective agreement. Ministers over there have not even read the bill properly. It is not often I feel sympathy with Liberals but I do feel a little sympathy for the defender of the Hamilton Ticats. I feel some sympathy for the men who try to keep Harold Ballard out of Hamilton. Here we have CUPW which comes under the public service act, under the jurisdiction of the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen), and lo and behold, the bill which affects them is being introduced by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro). I cannot help feeling sympathetic toward him if he feels beleaguered and asks: Good God, what nonentity wrote this bill and expects me to clean it up?
There is no protection in this bill for the workers. The post office flunkeys in middle management would love to see the workers without a collective agreement during those 60 or 90 days when an election is being held. They have never shown themselves to be particularly efficient in the absence of whatever is admirable in public relations. Again, the principle is one of confrontation. On the very day the CUPW negotiations went to conciliation, yesterday, the Prime Minister was tabling this bill in the House. Since the Minister of Labour seems to have done so well last Friday he wants to press his luck; he wants us to put the measure through today.
What sort of reaction, Mr. Speaker, do you think this will provoke in any honest-to-goodness trade union with any kind of balls? What kind of reaction might have been expected? I am amazed at the patience and restraint with which CUPW has reacted to Bill C-45. As I say, there is only one concept here, and that is confrontation.
There is political confrontation as well to some degree, because if there is one union in Canada which is not persona grata in the hearts and minds of the public from coast to coast it is CUPW. So the Prime Minister is trying to hoist the opposition in the House of Commons. What a marvellous election issue-to be able to go across the country and say: "We want to be sure there are no strikes in the post office during an election." And if other parties vote against it, he can
April 11, 1978

say: "The opposition tried to prevent us putting in that protection for you." This seems to me to be the height of cynicism and introduces an element of political confrontation.
For nine months CUPW has been without a contract from Treasury Board. Does anyone want to tell me that the Prime Minister got this sudden flash of insight only last week, that quite without premeditation he got the idea of bringing in a bill to make sure that CUPW would not go on strike during an election? Does anyone believe that the government has never foreseen that possibility in time to plan for it and to bring in a properly worded bill in time for it to be sent to committee where witnesses could be heard? Does anyone want to try to persuade me that the government was completely of far-sightedness in this respect? Mr. Speaker, this was planned. This was deliberate. This was cynical. This is confrontation politics and I cannot accept the principle which has been incorporated so blatantly in Bill C-45. I can see the minister shaking his head like a jack-in-the-box, but that is not what he was saying earlier today when he was stuck with this. He rolled out of bed this morning and said to his secretary: "Look what they have done."

Finally that friend of labour, Bryce Mackasey, said in my presence one morning at three o'clock that he would be prepared to lay a technological change clause on the table for CUPW. In the last ten years the government has changed postmasters general practically every year. I remember that in the first week the former postmaster general, who is now the Solicitor General (Mr. Blais), took over the post office he made a press statement. He said he would stay out of collective bargaining because he did not study labour law and was not a collective bargaining expert. One week later he was in there giving advice about the technological change clause, and the contract and about how the workers must live up to their responsibilities with regard to technological change. It was like Moses being taken out of the bullrushes! Suddenly overnight the new minister had become the expert. He was involving himself in the collective bargaining process.
I have listened to the Conservatives to my right. I can tell it is close to an election. They all love public servants. The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) was not kidding when he said there were many public servants in his riding. That was his reason for condemning the bill, but I want to see how he will vote on the principle of the bill.
I am sure all those who will be affected by the proposed Bill C-28 are anxious to see how the Conservatives will react. The Conservatives talk about studying the problems further. We do not need to study the problems any further. There has been royal commission after royal commission. The post office has been studied to death. Postmasters general have recommended that the post office be made a Crown corporation. They have said that that would provide some sense of continuity and unity of direction, instead of dealing with three or four departments and having a spread in jurisdiction. As a matter of fact, Eric Kierans, a former postmaster general, has said that the post office ought to be made a Crown corporation. That is what the workers have been harping about since I came to the House of Commons in 1972. They have said that they would prefer to be put under the aegis of the Canada Labour Code. Royal commission after royal commission has come to the same conclusion. There has been dilly-dallying, and these decisions which must be made have been put off.
Technological change has been brought in. We spent $1 billion to purchase equipment for the post office. The West Germans said they would be very happy to sell Canada the automated junk they sold us for $1 billion. One would think that that automated equipment would have speeded up mail service. Mail used to be put on trains. There were carriages at

the rear of those trains in which workers sorted mail. The mail was taken to the various communities and delivered. There was one-day service. The president of VIA, Frank Roberts, has spoken about going back to putting mail on trains. I asked Mr. Roberts if he envisaged the day when we would have a man sitting at a table in the carriage at the back of a VIA train sorting mail. He laughed. We have put in automated equipment, but that has not speeded up mail deliveries.
Somehow or other, the victim in that whole fiasco always seems to be the worker. By some means or other it is always the workers who are supposed to be delaying the mail, when in fact the government embarked on a very expensive technological change program in the post office. First of all, they did not know their elbows from a hole in the ground about how to work with the workers in the post office. I receive letters from postal locals right across the country. They write me about the problems they are having with their superiors in the post office. It seems to me that the middle management in the post office must have all been in the army at one time or another because they all seem to be the Colonel Jekyll and Colonel Hyde of the postal corps in the second world war and have no ideas, beyond barking orders to underlings, about how to handle workers on the floor. It is "yes, sir", or "no, sir", "don't question my authority, do as you are told and don't ask why". It seems to me that before the government embarked on this sort of technological process which involved changing the lives of workers, they should have been sent to some sort of humanizing schools to take a course on how to handle workers. Perhaps that is the first thing they should have done.
What they tried to do in the post office is to superimpose a technological operation and to fit square management personnel into round technological holes. It just did not work, and as a result tensions arose. For example, we went through the whole shamozzle in the last five years on the manner in which the Post Office Department uses casuals. That was one of the big fights that CUPW had. It was around the effective dealing with casuals in the post office. Invariably casuals had a "sweetheart arrangement" which involved every manager and his sweetheart getting jobs as casuals in the post office while other workers who had been casuals for ten or 15 years would be used in such a way that the contract or the terms of the collective agreement would not be followed with respect to those covered under the agreement. The workers had to put a lot of effort in to cleaning up the whole matter of casuals in the post office.
If the leadership in CUPW is militant, they have reason to be. We should look for the causes of their militancy; we cannot deal solely with the symptoms. They are symptoms of the frustration which emerges in what is called the angry leadership, the aggressive leadership. It seems to me that one of the causes for that relates to the way in which the post office is operated.
The former postmaster general-I have not heard the present Postmaster General (Mr. Lamontagne) on that-was

going to have these tete-a-tetes around the table. "You tell me your trouble, I will tell you mine. We will both put our problems on the table and we will then have two problems". We have not heard the Postmaster General go into that. The best way to have industrial harmony and peace in the work place is to clearly define the rights and responsibilities of the workers and of management in a contract which will be observed by both parties. That is the best way to maintain peace in the work place, instead of these little love-ins that are held so often, the net effect of which is to put off making tough decisions, which has the long term effect of sloughing off the problems to another day. "Let us have another cup of tea and talk about that problem again". The present minister has not been on to that kick yet, but I expect it will start coming shortly.
I know the leadership of CUPW very well. They are dedicated trade unionists who represent the interests of the workers. After all, it is the workers who have elected them, so whose interests should they represent? Surely not the interests of management. Their purpose is to ensure that the collective agreements are kept. We have a situation where there are literally thousands upon thousands of grievances that are backed up and have not been processed properly or expeditiously. That is one bone of contention in the relationship between management and workers in the post office.
What is the principle in this bill? As I have said, we deal with principles at second reading. I say that the principle in this bill is one of confrontation rather than solution of the problems that exist in the post office. This is confrontation politics. It is the principle of confrontation which is envisaged in this bill, and I and my party cannot support that. That is the other little game the government is playing. I do not think the Minister of Labour has participated in that Machiavellian scheme, but one of the aims of this bill is to try to hoist the NDP with the bill. In effect, how are the New Democrats going to react to that? Will they go along with such a blatant anti-labour bill? If we do that, it will wean our labour base from the party politics. I think the Minister of Labour has more principles than that. It is the other yahoos who occupy the government front benches for whom I have no respect, and I make no bones about it. I have never had any respect for them in the House because they are politicians in favour of whatever is going. Those are politics of convenience. In principle I could never support making scapegoats of one group of persons and using them for my own interests.
I am glad the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) is here. His record with respect to the nickel miners is not one to hold up as an example. If you have any principles at all, how can you go along with Bill C-45? Surely there is a principle involved there. How does one explain the fact that they did not even know that it did not cover the workers during the 60 day period under the collective agreement? Does that indicate to you a thoughtful and purposeful drafting of the
Postal Service
bill? Either the legal minds in that government are incompetent and should be fired or, as I said before, they are guilty of collusion to try to foist this bill on parliament in its dying days, to run it through while the boys are all busy talking about when the election will come so that they will not notice it. That is the kind of cynicism they are demonstrating.
We on this side of the House cannot support the principle involved in the bill and we intend to vote against the bill. If the minister wants to put CUPW under the protection and aegis of the Canada Labour Code, then do it and give them adequate notice. Do not put them under section 181 or section 148. Section 148 is the crux of the problem.
The minister stands up in the House and says there seems to be some confusion. I suggest the confusion is on the part of the minister and not in this opposition member's head. The confusion lies with cabinet ministers who are supposed to have such "smarts". They have less "smarts" than my pet Scottish terrier has in his tail.

subtopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE-ESTABLISHMENT OF GERIATRIC CHAIRS IN MEDICAL SCHOOLS
HEALTH AND WELFARE-ESTABLISHMENT OF GERIATRIC CHAIRS IN MEDICAL SCHOOLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 9 I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) a question concerning the increased demands made on health care as a result of the aging of the Canadian population. In particular, I asked her what steps were being taken to encourage the establishment of geriatric chairs in medical schools to train doctors in this special field.
I remember well that when I entered medicine pediatric teaching facilities were just being established, and what a difference they made to the mortality rate and to the number of hospital beds needed by the young. At the present time between 800 and 900 pediatricians are practising and doing excellent work. But the birth rate has swollen until today there are between 200,000 and 250,000 people aged 65 or over who are being cared for in institutions at a cost of $7,500,000 per day, or around $2 billion a year. The babies born during the post-war boom will be 65 and over by the year 2,000; by the turn of the century, based on present indications, there will be nearly four million people aged 65 or over. Economic strains may keep those people existing at poverty level unless they are allowed to continue to work as long as they wish to do so, contributing to society without restriction. The Americans now permit a man who is working and who wishes to continue to do
Adjournment Debate
so to carry on. Thus he has the additional advantage of feeling he is still useful.
A question which immediately comes to mind is this: Could three workers carry the extra load of two pensioners? The answer is: perhaps-if the proper training is given to doctors. Medical problems change as patients reach the age of 50 or more. As we age we may find we have more than one medical problem.
Geriatric medicine involves the treatment of the elderly and the maintenance of optimum health and mental and social aspects so that people may be returned to their own homes as quickly as possible. This is the reason for having geriatric chairs in the medical schools of Canada. Those who have a special aptitude for this and who are trained further in geriatric medicine departments should provide consultative services for older patients who occupy acute medical and surgical beds which are very expensive.
I might add that there may be a tendency to limit visits to the aged. No one has more reason than a doctor to dread old age, because during his professional career a doctor sees many of the worst features of this time of life. This may be one reason-and I have heard this many times-that doctors have an indifference toward older patients, while they might otherwise be excellent internists. However, doctors are far too ready to get old people into homes, often because of rising costs.
It is estimated that 75 to 80 per cent of the aged can remain in their own homes, while 15 per cent of those will require treatment, so they may need medical care and visits. Those who are experts in the geriatric field believe that of the 9 per cent of our population who are in homes today, 3 per cent could be in their own homes if some kind of home care was instituted. If we do not establish geriatric chairs at medical schools and if we continue as we are, we will not be able to provide beds for the elderly except by increasing health care costs and lowering the quality of medical care.
I want to thank the minister for writing to me on this subject. The minister shows an awareness of this very serious problem. Today we have only 27 trained geriatricians but 700 to 800 pediatricians. The time is now. Instead of 27, our need is for a minimum of 450 geriatricians across Canada. I hope the minister will take this to heart and keep the pressure on. Otherwise, this field will be neglected and people like you, Mr. Speaker, I and others in the House, as they get older, will all be in the old age group, and we will be the ones who will suffer.

subtopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE-ESTABLISHMENT OF GERIATRIC CHAIRS IN MEDICAL SCHOOLS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Rynard) for bringing this matter before the House once again. It is one of those questions of continuing concern to the hon. member, and I know also to the Department of National Health and Welfare and to the minister who has, on occasion, spoken on the matter eloquently. The minis-

April 11, 1978
Adjournment Debate
ter has also written to the hon. member suggesting how the matter can be dealt with properly.
As the hon. member knows, this whole question is in the realm of education which falls within the purview of the provinces. It is, therefore, rather difficult for the federal government or for the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) to decide unilaterally what to do, even though the minister may have a great desire to carry out the suggestions made by the hon. member, with which I personally agree, certainly in part and almost in toto. There is no question that the minister does have a role to play in this regard, and my understanding is that she is more than prepared to act as a catalyst so that the federal government can show leadership with regard to geriatrics, possibly by bringing various parties on the provincial level together with members of her department who also have the same concerns about geriatrics.
So I say to the hon. member that this matter is receiving consideration at present and will continue to receive it, and I thank him for bringing it before the House.

Mr. Speaker, two days ago I put a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) asking her if the government would reconsider its proposed ban on the sale of saccharin, which is to be implemented in the near future to limit the sale to drug stores and to take it out of grocery stores and other stores where it is at present being sold over the counter and in tablet form.
The House will recall that last year the Minister of National Health and Welfare released a report which suggested that tests in laboratory animals showed an increase in cancer caused by eating massive doses of saccharin, which in turn caused bladder cancer in animals. The government acted by removing saccharin from cans of pop and food. In January of this year the health protection branch issued letter No. 518 which stated that saccharin would be removed from grocery stores as soon as an order in council is passed, and its sale will be limited to pharmacies only. I understand that it is proposed that later this year saccharin be removed from tablets and toothpaste as well. I understand that provincial pharmacies will interpret this decision in such a way that in many provinces saccharin will not only be placed in a controlled section in the pharmacy but will also be sold from behind and under the counter.
If the decision is actually carried out by the government, it will cause a great deal of inconvenience to people on low carbohydrate diets, to diabetics, and especially to those living in the more remote areas of our country where there are no pharmacies or drug stores. If toothpaste and tablets and other such items which contain minute quantities of saccharin will have to be reformulated, this will result in a tremendous increase in the cost of these items to the consumer. I understand that it costs about $25,000 to bring in a substitute for

saccharin in pharmaceutical items. I believe that the government has exercised all due precaution by removing saccharin from pop and from foods, so that now it is available as a table top sweetener or in tablet form.
Studies which have been carried out in the United States, such as the inter-agency report put out in January of this year, did not deny or confirm that there were any harmful effects from saccharin to mice and certainly not to humans. In the United States an extensive study costing $1.4 million is being carried out this year to try to identify any harmful effects from the use of saccharin either on lab animals or on humans. Since reasonable caution has already been exercised, it seems to me we should not take the next step of limiting the sale of saccharin to pharmacies and taking it out of pharmaceuticals, where the amounts are minute, until we have further evidence from the studies which are being made in the United States and in other countries.
There are no proven harmful effects to humans from the use of saccharin. Indeed, I understand that one research project showed a lower level of bladder cancer in diabetics than in other people. So I think the government should wait until next year or until more proven results are shown of the harmful nature of saccharin. To remove it from general stores and limit it to drug stores at this time causes a great deal of inconvenience to consumers, especially in rural areas, to diabetics and to people on special low calorie diets.
I want to quote from a relevant study to show that no other country in the world has limited the use of saccharin in food, let alone restricted the sale of saccharin to drug stores. I want to quote from the German Cancer Research Center in Heidelberg, specifically Professor Dieter Schmahl, who had this to say after only two years of saccharin experiments with pregnant rats:
-the fact that it was even possible to apply a food additive in such large overdoses as in the Canadian experiment for a whole lifetime, attest mainly that it is not poisonous.
Let me also quote from the British Medical Journal, The Lancet. It states:
-the study by the Americans Wynder and Goldsmith which concluded that "users of saccharin have a smaller risk of bladder cancer than non users".
That is a very influential medical journal.
It seems to me it is premature, until more concrete evidence is laid before the scientific community, for the government to pass this order in council which will restrict the sale of saccharin to the drug store only. It is a product that has been on the market for many years. Thousands of tons of it in fact have been used by people who want to reduce their intake of sugar. I believe the health protection branch should consider this further before the government passes this order in council.

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-GOVERNMENT POLICY ON ACCEPTANCE OF NEUTRON BOMB
NATIONAL DEFENCE-GOVERNMENT POLICY ON ACCEPTANCE OF NEUTRON BOMB
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 5, I addressed a question to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Danson) concerning the government's position, or lack of one, in respect of the deployment of the neutron bomb by NATO. I then asked this supplementary question of the same minister:
Last Wednesday the minister said on television that we should give the neutron bomb to the Russians, ignoring the fact that it is not ours to give to anyone. Would the minister explain why he is so keen to give the neutron bomb to the Russians, when we ourselves seem incapable of deciding whether it should be deployed by NATO?
The minister answered by stating:
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member did a little more research in many areas, he might find out that that is not what I said.
I have a great deal of pride in the capabilities of my research staff and I resent the minister's ill-humoured remarks that he made on March 21 when the "Watson Report" was recorded for CBC television. I studied his words carefully before the "Watson Report" was aired and carefully read them after I watched the show live-partly because I could hardly believe what I had seen with my own eyes. The Minister of National Defence said this:
I think even in terms of-it might sound a little way out, but I rather like to start way out and then come down to earth-is on the reduced blast weapon or the enhanced radiation of the neutron bomb if you want to use the dirty word. But somehow, perhaps we should take this and give it to the Russians.
Adjournment Debate

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-GOVERNMENT POLICY ON ACCEPTANCE OF NEUTRON BOMB
speechtext: Give the neutron bomb to the Russians?

subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-GOVERNMENT POLICY ON ACCEPTANCE OF NEUTRON BOMB
speechtext:
Sure, we both have it.
Those, Mr. Speaker, were the minister's own words, and the crucial words were, when Mr. Watson asked: "Give the neutron bomb to the Russians?" and the minister replied: "Sure, we both have it." It is the minister who should do some research before he tries to pretend to the House of Commons that this was not what he said.
The fact is that the neutron bomb raises important issues for Canadians, as it does for all members of the NATO alliance. Not only must we as members of the alliance share a measure of responsibility for all alliance decisions, but we have 5,000 of our troops permanently stationed in central Europe, in positions which could be directly affected by decisions to deploy, and therefore one day to use, the neutron bomb.
Not only would the neutron bomb tend to lower the nuclear threshold and so threaten to make nuclear war more likely, it would almost certainly cause the Soviet Union to develop and deploy its own version of this weapon. I would estimate it would take only a couple of years for the Russians to be able to do that. Then we would be in a situation which would be fraught with even greater danger than the present, unstable enough "balance of terror" as far as nuclear weapons are concerned.
While using nuclear weapons remains a measurable and distinct step up the ladder of escalation, I believe their deterrent effect is preserved. If we introduce the neutron bomb this will change the situation. The Minister of National Defence either lacks the skill or the gumption to offer some indication to the Canadian people of what his government's views are on this question. This is peculiar to Canada. Other nations are discussing this matter. There has been wide public discussion in Germany, Belgium, Norway and the United States on this question. The minister of national defence in Belgium, in fact, resigned when he could not agree with his government's decision to deploy it.
The minister has in the past attempted to soften the reality of the debate on the neutron bomb by referring to it by such public relations names as "a reduced blast weapon" or "an enhanced radiation warhead". As everyone knows by now, this is a weapon which kills people at greater ranges than its blast destroys property or objects. For example, a one kiloton neutron bomb detonated as an air burst would emit fatal radiation for humans up to three-quarters of a mile away, while the blast and heat damage would perhaps extend for only 200 yards. Conventional warheads kill by blast and radiate heat with fallout as an unwanted byproduct. Neutron warheads kill by generating a sudden intense pulse of high velocity neutrons.
While very heavy neutron doses will incapacitate humans within a few minutes, they will not necessarily die for 24 to 48 hours. They will exhibit symptoms of convulsions, trembling, lack of muscular co-ordination, severe difficulty in breathing and intermittent stupor. There is no medical treatment. Those who receive less heavy, but nevertheless fatal, doses of neutrons will be initially incapacitated also within a few minutes, but will recover partially within half to three quarters of an

April 11, 1978
Adjournment Debate
hour. They will suffer nausea, fever, loss of appetite and extreme fatigue. Death may occur within four to six days as a result of massive infection and circulatory collapse. Once again there is no effective medical treatment.
The prospect of this latter group wandering around the combat zones-and they may include civilians as well as military-quite literally like an army of living dead is disturbing, not only on grounds of common humanity, but also in terms of military discipline, morale and military efficiency. To add to the all-round unpleasantness of this weapon, the neutron flux emitted by such a bomb is not invisible but can hardly be sensed except when very heavy doses are received, and then the victim feels a momentary tingling sensation.
I tend to agree with an American general quoted in the press but who insisted on anonymity to protect himself. He believes that neutron warheads come terribly close to chemical weapons such as poison gas, and that they may be illegal under international agreements which our government is bound by.
It is for these reasons that I believe that a minister of national defence with any real sense of his obligations to parliament and the people of this country would see fit to provide some leadership on this matter, and by that I mean doing more than trying to make a neutron bomb sound less horrible by using such names as a "reduced blast" or "enhanced radiation" weapon. Furthermore, I fail to see why he should be permitted to evade serious questions on this topic by making facetious or stupid suggestions, such as offering to give an American bomb which is not ours to give to the Russians.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jacques Guilbault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: NATIONAL DEFENCE-GOVERNMENT POLICY ON ACCEPTANCE OF NEUTRON BOMB
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Canada has already spoken out in regard to the neutron bomb. The government was asked what position Canada was taking in NATO on the neutron bomb. While Canada has no plans to acquire such weapons, we have been participating in discussions at NATO headquarters in Brussels regarding the possible acquisition by certain NATO countries of enhanced radiation, reduced-blast nuclear weapons. These discussions are continuing.
The military usefulness of the weapon is not in question but, like our allies, Canada is also conscious that its possible acquisition raises complex questions which must be examined
with care. Any decision regarding these weapons will not be taken lightly.
In passing, I want to stress there has been an unusual amount of misinformation printed on the neutron bomb. Most of the available public reports cast this weapon as something new and awful; actually it is only awful. And at that, it is less awful than weapons it could replace. The only thing new about the neutron bomb is its name and its packaging.
To begin with, it is necessary to agree on a name in order to avoid confusion. On the basis of the technical details available, it seems more appropriate to call this device a reduced blast/ enhanced radiation weapon, or RB/ERW. It is certainly not a bomb and that name should no longer be used in this connection.
The RB/ERW is essentially a very small hydrogen device or fusion device. In simpler terms, being much smaller, its effects are also infinitely smaller. Moreover, the peculiarity of this type of nuclear weapon is that it makes it possible, through appropriate design, to graduate in various modes the quantity of energy of the three physical effects which are common to all nuclear weapons: blast, heat and radiation. The latter are sub-divided into prompt and delayed radiation. The design of the RB/ERW is such that the partition of the total balance of energy yielded at the moment of the explosion favours radiation at the expense of blast and heat.
The RB/ERW will kill crews of tanks, which are the main threat to NATO, by nuclear radiation. In covering the same intended target area with a standard nuclear weapon, civilian casualties and damage to property from blast and thermal effects in a congested region would be much greater.
The decision to produce the RB/ERW has been from the very beginning one for the United States. The Canadian government is fully conscious of the dilemma which President Carter has been facing in the last several months regarding the production of the RB/ERW and we see merit in deferring the decision. In our deliberations, the suggestion of placing the weapon in an arms control context has not troubled us and we are looking forward to participation in future consultation on this matter with our NATO allies.
